topic: Tighten BI description and metric limits
old:
The BI architecture follows a protected data-to-dashboard pipeline. PostgreSQL views such as bi\_finance\_daily, \seqsplit{bi\_user\_lifecycle\_daily,} bi\_coach\_ops\_daily, and bi\_client\_health\_daily prepare canonical daily metrics. TypeScript service modules in the admin panel read those views and normalize the results into dashboard contracts. React components then display summary cards, trend panels, risk


queues, cohort tables, finance details, and threshold alerts. API routes under /api/bi provide exports, saved views, snapshots, and scheduled digest execution.


The BI layer is deliberately separated from normal CRUD pages. CRUD pages manage individual records, while BI pages aggregate and interpret platform behavior. This separation reduces duplication and makes it clearer which parts of the panel are operational management and which parts are decision-support analytics. The v1 BI scope is also explicit: finance is gross-pack-sales oriented, lifecycle and cohort metrics depend on available history, risk queues are operational signals, and all BI access must remain admin-protected.
new:
The BI service modules read daily metric views, including \texttt{bi\_finance\_daily}, \texttt{bi\_user\_lifecycle\_daily}, \texttt{bi\_coach\_ops\_daily} and \texttt{bi\_client\_health\_daily}, then prepare dashboard data. Routes under \texttt{/api/bi} support exports, saved views, snapshots and digest-related operations. These are source-defined responsibilities; selected CSV, saved-view and population-label checks do not validate every aggregate or scheduled route.

The finance scope is primarily gross pack sales. Available history constrains lifecycle/cohort interpretation, and risk queues are operational indicators. The sandbox exclusion verified for the Transactions live total does not certify every BI finance aggregate; card payments, wallet ledger entries and coach payouts must remain distinct.

\subsection{Development Assistance and Review Procedure}

AI assistants, including Codex, supported repository inspection, implementation proposals, debugging, diagram drafts and report revision. Connected tools provided file, browser and selected backend context. These tools supplied material for review rather than proof that a feature was implemented, deployed or tested.

The review procedure compared generated claims with source files, examined changes and retained the relevant execution artifacts when checks were performed. Missing execution evidence remains explicit in the QA matrix. Generated documentation and mock-based tests cannot establish native behavior, provider outcomes or historical sprint completion.

The present report is maintained in LaTeX. Earlier document-generation scripts are part of the drafting history; their existence does not verify the current report's content or the application. Responsibility for accepting the implementation and academic claims remains with the author.

old: GoFit includes an automation layer implemented with n8n workflow exports located in \seqsplit{docs/automation/n8n/workflows.} These workflows are part of the product because they perform scheduled operational work that would otherwise require manual monitoring by coaches or administrators. The n8n layer is separate from the mobile application and the admin panel: it runs in a trusted automation environment, calls Supabase through REST endpoints, and creates persistent rows in the database.
new: Five n8n exports in \path{../docs/automation/n8n/workflows} define scheduled briefing, reminder and digest operations using backend REST calls. They require a separate privileged runtime. The exports establish intended queries and writes, without establishing active hosting or successful scheduled execution.

old: The v1 automation design uses self-hosted n8n Community Edition as the practical free option. Runtime secrets are injected through environment variables. SUPABASE\_URL identifies the backend project, \seqsplit{SUPABASE\_SERVICE\_ROLE\_KEY} allows controlled server-side access, and GROQ\_API\_KEY is required only by the AI Session Prep workflow. These secrets must never be committed to the repository, placed in mobile code, or exposed in client-side admin bundles.

The service-role credential belongs in that server boundary; the Groq credential is needed by AI Session Prep. Configuration instructions do not establish that secrets were securely provisioned or that a container is running.

The implementation also depends on a large set of libraries that provide navigation, state management, forms, validation, media capture, haptic feedback, animations, charts, video calls, localization, notifications, artificial intelligence, and administration-table behavior.
